title: CBSE Class 12 Accountancy · Practice paper 2
subject: Accountancy
label: Practice paper

secNames.A: Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies

instr: This question paper contains 34 questions. All questions are compulsory.
This question paper is divided into two parts, Part A and Part B.
Part A (Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies) is compulsory for all candidates.
In the board paper, Part B has two options: (i) Analysis of Financial Statements and (ii) Computerised Accounting. This practice paper gives Option I, Analysis of Financial Statements.
Questions 1 to 16 and 27 to 30 carry 1 mark each.
Questions 17 to 20, 31 and 32 carry 3 marks each.
Questions 23 to 26 and 34 carry 6 marks each. Question 24 is a case-based question with six sub-parts of 1 mark each (multiple choice in the board paper; short answers here).
Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Sunita, a partner, withdrew ₹5,000 at the end of every month during the year ended 31st March 2026. Interest on drawings is charged @ 12% p.a. The interest on her drawings will be:
questions.sol: Total drawings = 5,000 × 12 = ₹60,000. For equal drawings at the end of every month, the average period is 5.5 months. Interest = 60,000 × 12/100 × 5.5/12 = ₹3,300.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Seema, a partner, is entitled to a commission of 5% of the net profit after charging such commission. The net profit of the firm before charging the commission is ₹2,52,000. Seema's commission will be:
questions.sol: Commission after charging such commission = 2,52,000 × 5/105 = ₹12,000. (5% of ₹2,52,000 = ₹12,600 would be commission before charging it.)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): A debentureholder is an owner of the company.
Reason (R): Debentureholders receive interest at a fixed rate on the face value of their debentures.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is correct explanation to (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not correct explanation of (A).
questions.sol: A debenture is an acknowledgement of a debt, so a debentureholder is a creditor of the company, not an owner. (A) is false. (R) is correct: debentures carry a fixed rate of interest.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Tara Ltd. issued 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, and the full amount was called up. All the money was received except the final call of ₹2 per share on 1,500 shares. The amount shown as 'Subscribed but not fully paid' capital in the Notes to Accounts will be:
questions.sol: Subscribed but not fully paid = 1,500 shares × ₹10 = ₹15,000, less calls in arrears 1,500 × 2 = ₹3,000, giving ₹12,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: P and Q share profits in the ratio of 3 : 2. They decide to share future profits in the ratio of 2 : 3. The Balance Sheet shows a debit balance of ₹30,000 in Profit and Loss Account (accumulated loss). The partners do not want to disturb this balance in the books. The adjusting entry will be:
options: P's Capital A/c Dr. ₹6,000; To Q's Capital A/c ₹6,000
Q's Capital A/c Dr. ₹6,000; To P's Capital A/c ₹6,000
P's Capital A/c Dr. ₹18,000 and Q's Capital A/c Dr. ₹12,000; To Profit and Loss A/c ₹30,000
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To P's Capital A/c ₹18,000 and To Q's Capital A/c ₹12,000
questions.sol: The loss belongs to the old ratio: P ₹18,000, Q ₹12,000. If it stays in the books it will later be borne in the new ratio: P ₹12,000, Q ₹18,000. So P must bear ₹6,000 more now and Q ₹6,000 less: P's Capital A/c Dr. ₹6,000 To Q's Capital A/c ₹6,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A and B are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 5 : 3. They admit C, and the new profit sharing ratio of A, B and C is 4 : 2 : 2. The sacrificing ratio of A and B is:
questions.sol: A's sacrifice = 5/8 − 4/8 = 1/8; B's sacrifice = 3/8 − 2/8 = 1/8. Sacrificing ratio = 1 : 1.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: X and Y are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 3 : 2. They admit Z for 1/4th share in profits. Goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹1,60,000. Z cannot bring his share of goodwill premium in cash, so it is adjusted through his Current Account. The amount credited to X's Capital Account for goodwill will be:
questions.sol: Z's share of goodwill = 1,60,000 × 1/4 = ₹40,000. It is credited to X and Y in their sacrificing ratio, which is the old ratio 3 : 2 (nothing else is given). X gets 40,000 × 3/5 = ₹24,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A, B and C are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 2 : 2 : 1. B retires, and his share is taken over by A and C in the ratio of 3 : 2. The new profit sharing ratio of A and C will be:
questions.sol: B's share 2/5 is taken 3 : 2: A gets 6/25 and C gets 4/25. A = 2/5 + 6/25 = 16/25; C = 1/5 + 4/25 = 9/25. New ratio = 16 : 9.
questions.chapter: Retirement and Death of a Partner

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: D, a partner, died during the year. The following items appear in his capital account at the time of settlement: opening capital ₹1,50,000, share of goodwill ₹30,000, share of loss on revaluation ₹6,000, share of general reserve ₹12,000 and drawings ₹8,000. The amount payable to D's executors will be:
questions.sol: Amount payable = 1,50,000 + 30,000 (goodwill) + 12,000 (reserve) − 6,000 (revaluation loss) − 8,000 (drawings) = ₹1,78,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the dissolution of a firm, assets (other than cash) of ₹3,00,000 and creditors of ₹80,000 were transferred to the Realisation Account. The assets realised ₹2,40,000, creditors were paid ₹76,000 in full settlement and realisation expenses were ₹4,000. The result of realisation is:
questions.sol: Debit side: assets 3,00,000 + creditors paid 76,000 + expenses 4,000 = ₹3,80,000. Credit side: creditors 80,000 + assets realised 2,40,000 = ₹3,20,000. Loss = 3,80,000 − 3,20,000 = ₹60,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, were forfeited after the holder had paid ₹7 per share. The minimum price per share at which these shares can be reissued as fully paid up is:
questions.sol: The discount allowed on reissue cannot exceed the amount forfeited (₹7 per share). Minimum reissue price = 10 − 7 = ₹3 per share.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Shares issued by a company to its employees or directors at a discount, or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how or making available rights such as intellectual property rights are called:
questions.sol: These are sweat equity shares. Under ESOP, employees get an option to buy shares later at a fixed price; bonus shares are issued free out of reserves; right shares are offered to existing shareholders.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A company issued 2,000 debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 6%, redeemable at a premium of 5%. The amount of loss on issue of these debentures is:
questions.sol: Loss on issue = discount on issue (2,000 × 6 = ₹12,000) + premium payable on redemption (2,000 × 5 = ₹10,000) = ₹22,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On dissolution, Asha, a partner, agreed to take over the work of dissolution and bear all realisation expenses for a remuneration of ₹10,000. The actual realisation expenses of ₹12,000 were paid by the firm on her behalf. The entry for payment of these expenses will be:
options: Realisation A/c Dr. ₹12,000; To Bank A/c ₹12,000
Asha's Capital A/c Dr. ₹12,000; To Bank A/c ₹12,000
Realisation A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Bank A/c ₹10,000
Realisation A/c Dr. ₹2,000; To Asha's Capital A/c ₹2,000
questions.sol: Asha has to bear the expenses, so the amount paid by the firm on her behalf is debited to her capital account. (Her remuneration of ₹10,000 is recorded separately: Realisation A/c Dr. To Asha's Capital A/c.)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: When the capitals of partners are fixed, which of the following is recorded in the partners' Current Accounts?
questions.sol: Under the fixed capital method, the capital account records only the opening capital, additional capital introduced and permanent withdrawal of capital. Interest on drawings, like drawings, salary and share of profit, goes to the current account.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Aditi and Bhavna are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio of 3 : 1. Their Balance Sheet on 31st March 2026 was:
Balance Sheet of Aditi and Bhavna as at 31st March 2026

Capital: Bhavna1,20,000Furniture1,60,000

On 1st April 2026 they admit Chetan for 1/5th share in future profits on these terms:
1. Chetan brings ₹1,50,000 as his capital and his share of goodwill premium in cash. Goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹2,00,000.
2. The market value of investments is ₹74,000.
3. Furniture is to be depreciated by 10%.
4. Stock is to be valued at ₹1,20,000.
5. An expense of ₹2,000 is outstanding but not recorded.
6. Revised values are to be shown in the books. There is no information about how Chetan acquires his share from the old partners.
Answer the following on the basis of the above information.

parts.q: (i) Calculate the new profit sharing ratio of Aditi, Bhavna and Chetan.
parts.model: Remaining share = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5, shared by Aditi and Bhavna in 3 : 1. Aditi = 3/4 × 4/5 = 3/5; Bhavna = 1/4 × 4/5 = 1/5; Chetan = 1/5. New ratio = 3 : 1 : 1.

New ratio 3 : 1 : 1

parts.q: (ii) Calculate Chetan's share of goodwill premium and show how it will be distributed.
parts.model: Chetan's premium = 2,00,000 × 1/5 = ₹40,000. It is credited in the sacrificing ratio, which is the old ratio 3 : 1: Aditi ₹30,000, Bhavna ₹10,000.

Aditi ₹30,000 and Bhavna ₹10,000 (sacrificing ratio 3 : 1)

parts.q: (iii) How much of the Investment Fluctuation Reserve will be credited to the old partners, and how much to each?
parts.model: Fall in value of investments = 80,000 − 74,000 = ₹6,000, met from the reserve. Balance of reserve = 12,000 − 6,000 = ₹6,000, credited in the old ratio: Aditi ₹4,500, Bhavna ₹1,500.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Which of the following is shown under the sub-head 'Short-term Provisions' in the Balance Sheet of a company?
questions.sol: Provision for tax is a short-term provision. Unpaid dividend is an other current liability, bills payable are trade payables, and provision for doubtful debts is deducted from trade receivables.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): A high inventory turnover ratio generally shows efficient management of inventory.
Reason (R): Inventory turnover ratio is calculated by dividing revenue from operations by average trade receivables.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
questions.sol: A is correct: a high ratio means inventory is sold quickly. R is incorrect: inventory turnover ratio = cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory. Revenue ÷ average trade receivables is the trade receivables turnover ratio.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Which of the following is a cash equivalent while preparing a Cash Flow Statement?
options: Treasury bills maturing within three months of acquisition
Equity shares held as a long-term investment
questions.sol: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value, generally with a maturity of three months or less from acquisition. Treasury bills of three months qualify.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
From the following information, calculate:
(i) Trade Receivables Turnover Ratio
(ii) Gross Profit Ratio
(iii) Inventory Turnover Ratio
(iv) Working Capital Turnover Ratio
Goods are sold at a gross profit of 25% on cost.
ParticularsAmount (₹)
Revenue from operations (of which credit sales ₹6,00,000)8,00,000
Trade receivables: opening1,40,000
Trade receivables: closing1,60,000
Inventory: opening70,000
Inventory: closing90,000
Current assets (closing)4,00,000
Current liabilities (closing)2,00,000
questions.model:
(i) Average trade receivables = (1,40,000 + 1,60,000)/2 = ₹1,50,000. Trade Receivables Turnover Ratio = Credit revenue from operations/Average trade receivables = 6,00,000/1,50,000 = 4 times.
(ii) Gross profit = 25% on cost = 20% on sales; cost of revenue from operations = 8,00,000 × 100/125 = ₹6,40,000; gross profit = ₹1,60,000. Gross Profit Ratio = 1,60,000/8,00,000 × 100 = 20%.
(iii) Average inventory = (70,000 + 90,000)/2 = ₹80,000. Inventory Turnover Ratio = 6,40,000/80,000 = 8 times.
(iv) Working capital = 4,00,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. Working Capital Turnover Ratio = 8,00,000/2,00,000 = 4 times.

points.t: (i) Trade Receivables Turnover Ratio = 4 times (credit sales ÷ average receivables ₹1,50,000)
(ii) Gross Profit Ratio = 20% (cost ₹6,40,000; gross profit ₹1,60,000)
(iii) Inventory Turnover Ratio = 8 times (₹6,40,000 ÷ ₹80,000)
(iv) Working Capital Turnover Ratio = 4 times (₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000)
